name: SearXNG
description: Self-hostable metasearch engine aggregating results from many search services and databases without tracking or profiling users.
journalism_use_case: Run queries across dozens of engines from one self-hosted instance, compare result sets, and avoid personalised/filtered results during research.
deployment: docker / self-hosted web app; public instances exist
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-15 per GitHub API; 39,595 stars
platform_api_risk: Depends on scraping/APIs of upstream engines; individual engines break or rate-limit frequently and must be disabled per-instance.
external_deps: Upstream search engines; optional API keys for some engines
data_flows: Queries leave your instance to upstream engines; self-hosting keeps query logs local
opsec_notes: Self-host or use a trusted instance: a public instance operator sees all your queries. Instance IP is visible to upstream engines, so a dedicated instance can still fingerprint an investigation.
limitations: Result completeness varies by engine health; no persistent archiving of results.

name: YaCy
description: Peer-to-peer and intranet search engine that crawls and indexes sites you choose, with its own index rather than third-party results.
journalism_use_case: Build a private searchable index over a defined set of target sites (ministries, forums, company sites) for repeatable full-text investigation.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-03 per GitHub API; 4,110 stars; COPYRIGHT states GPL (LGPL for files in source/net/yacy/cora)
platform_api_risk: No dependence on commercial search APIs; crawling is subject to robots.txt and site blocking.
data_flows: Crawled content stored locally; P2P mode shares index fragments with other peers
opsec_notes: P2P mode exposes your index/queries to the network — run in intranet/private mode for sensitive work. Your crawler hits targets directly from your IP.
limitations: Heavy resource use; relevance ranking weaker than commercial engines; UI dated.

name: Marginalia Search
description: Independent search engine and crawler indexing text-oriented, small, old and non-commercial websites, with full source available.
journalism_use_case: Surface obscure personal pages, forums and old sites that mainstream engines suppress — useful for finding early traces of a person or organisation.
deployment: hosted public instance; self-hosting possible but index build is heavy
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-14 per GitHub API; 2,239 stars; LICENSE.md text is GNU Affero General Public License v3
platform_api_risk: None — own crawler and index, no third-party search API dependency.
data_flows: Queries to the public instance go to the operator; self-hosted keeps everything local
opsec_notes: Public instance sees queries; no login required. Self-hosting is the only way to keep sensitive query patterns private.
limitations: Deliberately partial index (de-prioritises commercial web); not a Google replacement.

name: 4get
description: Self-hostable proxy metasearch engine in PHP that scrapes and reformats results from multiple upstream engines, including images and video.
journalism_use_case: Query several engines without logging in or running JavaScript, and compare how different engines rank the same target.
deployment: Apache2 or Docker self-hosting; public instance at 4get.ca
activity_evidence: Most recent commit shown 2026-11-15 19:41 ('forgot settings woopsies', 4c7c4ea072) on git.lolcat.ca; licence stated as AGPLv3-only
platform_api_risk: Pure scraping of upstream engines — individual scrapers break when engines change markup or add bot defences.
data_flows: Your instance proxies queries to upstream engines; public instance operator sees queries
opsec_notes: Self-host for sensitive queries; public instances are run by unknown third parties. Scraping may breach upstream engines' ToS.
limitations: Not on GitHub (self-hosted forge), smaller contributor base than SearXNG; scraper breakage is routine.

name: LibreY
description: JavaScript-free privacy-respecting metasearch engine and framework, a maintained continuation of the LibreX project.
journalism_use_case: Lightweight self-hosted meta-search for quick multi-engine checks when a full SearXNG deployment is overkill.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-06-10 per GitHub API; 327 stars
platform_api_risk: Scrapes upstream engines; subject to the same breakage as other metasearch scrapers.
data_flows: Queries proxied to upstream engines
opsec_notes: Public instances see your queries; scraping upstream engines may violate their ToS.
limitations: Smaller engine coverage and slower cadence than SearXNG (5 months since last push).

name: Whoogle Search
description: Self-hosted, ad-free front-end that returned Google results without tracking, cookies or JavaScript requirements.
journalism_use_case: Historically used to query Google without a personalised session; now mainly a reference for why self-hosted Google front-ends are no longer viable.
activity_evidence: Repository is archived (GitHub API archived=true); last push 2026-08-14; 11,551 stars
platform_api_risk: Effectively broken: README states Google blocked no-JS results and that the Custom Search Engine fallback 'is no longer viable', with no need to open issues about it.
external_deps: Google (scraping) or paid Google Custom Search API (100 free queries/day then paid)
data_flows: Queries proxied from your instance to Google
opsec_notes: Instance IP becomes the fingerprint Google sees; shared public instances leak your queries to the operator.
limitations: Archived and dependent on a scraping path Google has closed.

name: pagodo
description: Automated Google dorking: scraped the Google Hacking Database then ran those dork queries at scale against targets.
journalism_use_case: Reference implementation of bulk dorking workflows; its GHDB scraper still documents dork syntax useful for manual searching.
activity_evidence: Archived (GitHub API archived=true); README: 'This repository is archived and no longer maintained... archived on November 1, 2026'
platform_api_risk: Effectively broken: README states Google changed how search results are returned in July/August 2026, rendering the yagooglesearch library unreliable; upstream googlesearch was archived 2026-02-13.
data_flows: Dork queries issued directly to Google from your IP
opsec_notes: Bulk automated dorking gets your IP blocked/captcha'd, signals your interest to anyone correlating logs, and breaches Google ToS.
limitations: Automated Google dorking is broadly non-functional as of late 2026 — treat dorking as a manual technique.

name: dorks_hunter
description: Simple Google dorks search tool that runs a curated dork set against a target domain.
journalism_use_case: One of the few dorking helpers still receiving commits after pagodo's archival, for quick exposed-file discovery on a domain.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-07-14 per GitHub API; 350 stars; GitHub API reports no licence and no licence/COPYING file exists in the repository root (verified via contents API)
platform_api_risk: Same structural problem as pagodo: depends on Google result scraping, which Google disrupted in mid-2026 — expect unreliable or empty results.
data_flows: Dork queries issued to Google from your IP
opsec_notes: No licence declared, so newsroom redistribution is legally unclear; automated querying breaches Google ToS and risks IP blocking.
limitations: Unlicensed; reliability now bounded by Google's 2026 anti-scraping changes.

name: Metabigor
description: OSINT collection CLI that queries multiple public sources (search engines, network/ASN and certificate data) without requiring API keys.
journalism_use_case: Quickly map an organisation's internet footprint (netblocks, ASNs, related hosts) from public sources before deeper investigation.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-08-08 per GitHub API; 1,870 stars
platform_api_risk: Relies on scraping third-party sites that change without notice; individual modules degrade silently.
data_flows: Queries sent from your host to third-party services
opsec_notes: Queries originate from your IP and may be logged by the queried services; use network separation for sensitive targets.
limitations: Infrastructure-oriented rather than social-media oriented; output needs manual validation.

name: uncover
description: CLI that queries multiple internet-wide scan search engines (Shodan, Censys, Fofa, Hunter, Zoomeye and others) through one interface.
journalism_use_case: Find exposed servers, cameras or panels tied to an entity under investigation across several scan databases with one query.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-09 per GitHub API; 3,116 stars
platform_api_risk: Each engine requires its own API key and most have strict free-tier quotas; results depend on commercial data subscriptions.
external_deps: API keys for Shodan/Censys/Fofa/Hunter/Zoomeye etc., several paid
data_flows: Your queries and target identifiers are sent to commercial scan vendors
opsec_notes: Vendors log queries against your API key and identity — a real deanonymisation risk when researching sensitive targets.
limitations: Infrastructure focus; useful for entity-to-server mapping rather than social research.

name: Zoekplaatje
description: Firefox extension that captures search engine result pages as structured data while you browse, for later analysis.
journalism_use_case: Document what a search engine actually showed, when, and in what order — evidence for algorithmic-bias and disinformation-ranking stories.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-06 per GitHub API; 14 stars; LICENSE file states Mozilla Public License v2.0
platform_api_risk: Parsers must track each engine's HTML; capture silently stops when a SERP layout changes.
external_deps: Firefox; the search engines you visit
data_flows: Captured SERP data stored locally in the browser and exported by the user
opsec_notes: Captures run in your own logged-in browser session — use a clean profile so personalised results and your identity are not entangled with the capture.
limitations: Small user base; Firefox-only; engine coverage limited to implemented parsers.

name: name-variant-search
description: Browser tool that generates common variations and transliterations of a human name for use in search queries.
journalism_use_case: Expand searches for a person whose name is transliterated inconsistently across Russian, Ukrainian, Arabic or other scripts.
deployment: static web app (GitHub Pages) or local
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-06-25 per GitHub API; 56 stars
platform_api_risk: None — no platform APIs involved.
data_flows: Name input processed client-side in the hosted static page
opsec_notes: Using the hosted page means the name is typed into a Bellingcat-hosted site; run locally if the subject's name is itself sensitive.
limitations: Heuristic variant generation only; no search execution or results.

name: OSINT Framework
description: Interactive tree-based directory of OSINT resources and tools organised by data type and investigative goal.
journalism_use_case: Starting point for choosing a collection method or source type when you know the identifier you hold but not the tooling.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-10-31 per GitHub API; 12,464 stars
platform_api_risk: Index entries rot as linked tools die; it links to many dead or hosted-only services.
external_deps: Third-party tools and sites it links to
data_flows: No investigative data flows; it is a link index
opsec_notes: Clicking through to third-party hosted tools exposes your identifiers to those operators — check each destination before pasting target data.
limitations: Directory, not a tool; link quality and freshness vary widely.

name: CouncilSearcher
description: Open tool for finding verbatim quotes in UK and Ireland council meeting records.
journalism_use_case: Local-government accountability reporting: find what a named councillor actually said about an issue across many meeting transcripts.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-01-07 per GitHub API; 17 stars
platform_api_risk: Depends on council websites' publication formats; individual councils break ingestion.
data_flows: Fetches public council records to local storage
opsec_notes: Low risk: requests go to public-sector sites; no account needed.
limitations: Scoped to UK/Ireland; small project, 10 months since last push.

name: katana
description: Next-generation crawling and spidering framework with standard and headless modes, JS parsing and flexible scope control.
journalism_use_case: Enumerate every reachable page and document on a target site (PDFs, archives, staging paths) before mirroring or analysis.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-16 per GitHub API; 17,856 stars
platform_api_risk: None platform-specific; aggressive crawling triggers WAF/Cloudflare blocking.
data_flows: Direct HTTP(S) requests from your host to the target
opsec_notes: Crawl traffic is highly visible in the target's logs and attributable to your IP; throttle and consider whether the target should know you are looking.
limitations: Discovers URLs rather than preserving content — pair with a WARC capture tool for evidence.

name: Scrapy
description: Mature high-level Python framework for writing web crawlers and structured scrapers at scale.
journalism_use_case: Build repeatable bulk collection of structured public records (court listings, registries, classifieds) into datasets for analysis.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-13 per GitHub API; 65,427 stars
platform_api_risk: Not platform-specific, but scraping logged-in social platforms with it generally breaches their ToS and breaks often.
data_flows: Requests from your infrastructure to targets; data stored locally
opsec_notes: Requires engineering discipline on rate limits and user agents; careless crawls are traceable and can harm small sites.
limitations: Developer tool: no UI, no archiving/evidentiary output by default.

name: Crawlee
description: Node.js/TypeScript crawling and browser-automation library supporting Playwright, Puppeteer, Cheerio and raw HTTP with proxy rotation.
journalism_use_case: Collect JavaScript-heavy public pages (dynamic dashboards, infinite-scroll listings) that simple HTTP crawlers cannot render.
deployment: npm library; runs locally or on Apify platform
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-16 per GitHub API; 26,464 stars
platform_api_risk: Built-in proxy rotation is often used to evade platform anti-bot controls — ethically and legally sensitive, and ToS-violating on most social platforms.
external_deps: Node.js, browsers; optional paid proxy providers and Apify cloud
data_flows: Target requests via your host or third-party proxies; proxy vendors see target URLs
opsec_notes: Commercial proxy use routes your collection through third parties who log it; vendor-funded development means defaults favour the hosted platform.
limitations: Engineering-heavy; no investigative UI or evidence packaging.

name: HTTrack
description: Long-established website copier that mirrors a site to local disk with rewritten links for offline browsing.
journalism_use_case: Take a quick offline mirror of a site likely to be edited or taken down, for later reading and keyword search.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-16 per GitHub API; 4,840 stars
platform_api_risk: Pre-JavaScript-era design: fails on SPA/social sites and anything behind bot protection.
data_flows: Direct downloads from target to local disk
opsec_notes: Default user agent and crawl pattern are easily recognised; mirrors carry no cryptographic integrity metadata.
limitations: Produces a loose file tree, not WARC — weak as evidence of record; poor with dynamic sites.

name: SiteOne Crawler
description: Cross-platform website crawler and analyser that produces structured site reports and can export a browsable offline copy.
journalism_use_case: Inventory a target site's structure, assets and third-party components, and keep an offline copy for reference.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-09-27 per GitHub API; 1,010 stars
platform_api_risk: Not platform-dependent; subject to bot blocking on protected sites.
data_flows: Direct crawl of target; reports written locally
opsec_notes: Crawl is visible to the target; marketed for SEO/devops so the traffic pattern is unremarkable.
limitations: Analysis/export focus rather than archival WARC output; vendor-led project.

name: Photon
description: Fast crawler designed for OSINT that extracts URLs, emails, social handles, files, secrets and parameters from crawled pages.
journalism_use_case: Harvest contact details, document links and handles scattered across a target website in a single pass.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-10-17 per GitHub API; 13,346 stars
platform_api_risk: Optional Wayback Machine seeding depends on the IA CDX API; no social platform APIs.
data_flows: Crawls target directly; results written to local JSON/text
opsec_notes: Extraction of 'secrets' can pull credentials into your working directory — handle findings carefully and do not use them.
limitations: Light maintenance cadence relative to its age; no JS rendering.

name: Hyphe
description: Research web crawler with a control interface that builds curated corpora of websites and maps the hyperlink network between them.
journalism_use_case: Map an ecosystem — e.g. a disinformation or lobbying network — by curating which sites belong to the corpus and visualising how they link.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-05-18 per GitHub API; 392 stars
platform_api_risk: Crawls the open web only; social platforms are largely uncrawlable, so coverage skews to websites.
data_flows: Crawled pages and link graph stored in your instance
opsec_notes: Self-hosting keeps corpus definitions private; the public demo instance should not be used for sensitive corpora.
limitations: Heavy install; six months since last push; curation is manual and labour-intensive.

name: Heritrix 3
description: The Internet Archive's extensible, web-scale, archival-quality crawler, writing standards-compliant WARC output.
journalism_use_case: Large-scale archival crawls of whole domains where the capture must be WARC-based and defensible.
deployment: self-hosted JVM service with web admin UI
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-14 per GitHub API; 3,351 stars; GitHub reports NOASSERTION but the LICENSE file text is the Apache License 2.0
platform_api_risk: Non-browser crawler: modern JS-heavy and social sites are captured poorly compared with browser-based crawlers.
data_flows: WARCs written to your storage
opsec_notes: Crawl volume is conspicuous; requires operator competence to avoid overloading targets.
limitations: Steep learning curve; weak on dynamic content — use Browsertrix Crawler for high-fidelity social captures.

name: brozzler
description: Distributed browser-based web crawler that drives real Chrome instances and records traffic to WARC via warcprox.
journalism_use_case: Archive JavaScript-dependent pages at scale where a plain crawler would capture empty shells.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-14 per GitHub API; 824 stars
platform_api_risk: Browser-driven so handles JS, but logged-in social capture remains ToS-sensitive and brittle.
data_flows: Captured traffic proxied through warcprox into WARC files you hold
opsec_notes: Browser profiles can leak identity if cookies/logins are reused; use dedicated profiles per investigation.
limitations: Operationally complex multi-service deployment; IA-internal priorities drive development.

name: grab-site
description: Archivist's crawler producing WARC output with a live dashboard and dynamically adjustable ignore patterns during a crawl.
journalism_use_case: Rapid-response archiving of a site at risk of deletion, with the ability to steer the crawl while it runs.
deployment: pip / local CLI with web dashboard
activity_evidence: Last push 2025-05-23 per GitHub API; 1,617 stars; LICENSE file is MIT text ('Copyright (c) 2015 Ivan Kozik')
platform_api_risk: Non-browser crawl; poor fidelity on JS-driven and bot-protected sites.
data_flows: WARC + logs written locally
opsec_notes: Visible crawl from your IP; no built-in integrity signing of WARCs.
limitations: 18 months since last push; depends on wpull, itself last pushed 2024-04.

name: wpull
description: Wget-compatible downloader and crawler with WARC output, used as the engine beneath grab-site.
journalism_use_case: Wget-style recursive capture when you need WARC output and wget's familiar flag semantics.
activity_evidence: Last push 2024-04-29 per GitHub API (over 18 months stale); 613 stars; not marked archived
platform_api_risk: No platform APIs; fails on JS-heavy sites.
data_flows: WARC written locally
opsec_notes: Stale dependency chain can carry unpatched libraries — isolate the environment.
limitations: Effectively dormant; prefer browsertrix-crawler or wget --warc for new work.

name: ArchiveBot
description: IRC-driven bot infrastructure that coordinates volunteer archiving of websites into WARC collections.
journalism_use_case: Mobilise community archiving capacity when a large site must be preserved faster than one newsroom can manage.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-09-08 per GitHub API; 429 stars
platform_api_risk: Depends on ArchiveTeam's volunteer infrastructure and Internet Archive ingestion.
external_deps: IRC network, ArchiveTeam pipelines, Internet Archive
data_flows: Captures are ingested into public ArchiveTeam/IA collections — not private
opsec_notes: Requests are public in IRC channels: asking for a site to be archived publicly signals your interest in that target.
limitations: Not a private tool; you are requesting work from a community, with public logs.

name: pywb
description: Core Python web archiving toolkit providing recording and high-fidelity replay of WARC/WACZ collections, including a self-hosted Wayback.
journalism_use_case: Stand up your own wayback-style replay server over captured WARCs so the newsroom can cite and revisit evidence independently.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-16 per GitHub API; 1,720 stars
platform_api_risk: Replay fidelity of social platforms depends on how well the original capture handled JS; not an API consumer itself.
data_flows: Serves only archives you hold; no external calls needed
opsec_notes: Self-hosted replay avoids revealing to a third-party archive which pages you are studying — a real advantage over querying the public Wayback Machine.
limitations: Operator skill needed; replay of heavily dynamic captures can still be imperfect.

name: ArchiveBox
description: Self-hosted web archiving system that takes URLs from bookmarks, history or feeds and saves HTML, JS, PDF, screenshots, media and WARC.
journalism_use_case: Maintain a searchable newsroom archive of every source page cited in a story, captured in several formats at once.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-16 per GitHub API; 29,034 stars
platform_api_risk: Social-media capture quality varies and degrades as platforms add login walls; leans on yt-dlp and headless Chrome for media.
external_deps: Chromium, yt-dlp, wget, optional singlefile/readability extractors
data_flows: Captures stored locally; some extractors call the live web and optionally archive.org
opsec_notes: Config can submit URLs to archive.org, publicly disclosing what you are archiving — review the archive.org extractor setting before sensitive work.
limitations: Multi-extractor stack is maintenance-heavy; not designed as a chain-of-custody evidence system.

name: Browsertrix Crawler
description: High-fidelity browser-based archiving crawler in a single Docker container, producing WARC/WACZ with behaviour scripts for dynamic sites.
journalism_use_case: Capture social-media pages, maps and dashboards as they actually appear, in a replayable archive-of-record format.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-14 per GitHub API; 1,197 stars
platform_api_risk: Captures what a browser sees, so login-walled platforms need a logged-in profile — raising ToS and account-safety issues; site behaviours need updating as platforms change.
data_flows: WARC/WACZ written to local volume; no upload unless configured
opsec_notes: If you supply an authenticated browser profile, your account identity is embedded in the capture session and may be flagged or banned — use dedicated research accounts.
limitations: Resource-hungry; per-site behaviours lag platform redesigns.

name: Browsertrix
description: Browser-based crawling and archiving service with multi-user orgs, scheduled crawls and collection management; self-hostable.
journalism_use_case: Team-scale archiving programme where multiple reporters schedule crawls and share replayable collections.
deployment: Kubernetes self-hosted, or Webrecorder-hosted paid service
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-14 per GitHub API; 500 stars
platform_api_risk: Same browser-capture constraints as Browsertrix Crawler for login-walled platforms.
external_deps: Kubernetes, S3-compatible storage; hosted plan is paid
data_flows: Crawls and WACZ stored in your cluster, or in Webrecorder's hosted service if using SaaS
opsec_notes: Hosted plan means a third party holds your capture targets and artefacts; self-host for sensitive investigations.
limitations: Kubernetes operational burden for self-hosting; small newsrooms usually end up on the paid service.

name: ArchiveWeb.page
description: Chrome/Chromium extension that records high-fidelity web archives of pages as you browse them, exporting WACZ/WARC.
journalism_use_case: Manually capture a social post, story or logged-in page exactly as seen, producing a replayable file for the evidence locker.
deployment: browser extension (Chrome Web Store) and desktop app
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-09 per GitHub API; 1,629 stars
platform_api_risk: Immune to API shutdowns because it captures the rendered DOM; capturing logged-in platform content may breach platform ToS.
data_flows: Archive stored in the browser profile until exported; nothing uploaded by default
opsec_notes: Captures include cookies/session artefacts from your own browsing: review before sharing a WACZ, since it can expose your accounts and identity.
limitations: Manual, one-page-at-a-time workflow; large captures strain browser storage.

name: ReplayWeb.page
description: Serverless, browser-based replay of WARC/WACZ web archives with no server infrastructure required.
journalism_use_case: Let editors, lawyers and readers open and inspect an archived page themselves, offline, from a single file.
deployment: static web app / local file; embeddable
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-14 per GitHub API; 1,015 stars
platform_api_risk: None — replays only what was captured.
data_flows: Replay happens entirely client-side; archives are not uploaded
opsec_notes: Because replay is local, sharing an archive does not reveal your research to any archive operator — but the archive itself may contain your session data.
limitations: Fidelity is bounded by the original capture; very large archives load slowly.

name: wabac.js
description: Web Archive Browsing Augmentation Client: the service-worker replay engine underneath ReplayWeb.page and ArchiveWeb.page.
journalism_use_case: Embed archive replay directly into a newsroom web application or story page without a replay server.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-13 per GitHub API; 130 stars
platform_api_risk: None.
external_deps: Modern browser with service worker support
data_flows: Client-side only
opsec_notes: AGPL-3.0 obligations apply if you embed it in a public-facing service.
limitations: Library-level component; not used directly by journalists.

name: browsertrix-behaviors
description: In-browser behaviour scripts that automatically interact with complex sites (scrolling, expanding, playing media) during archiving.
journalism_use_case: Make automated captures of infinite-scroll social feeds and video pages actually complete, rather than capturing the first screen.
deployment: npm package consumed by ArchiveWeb.page and Browsertrix Crawler
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-10 per GitHub API; 60 stars
platform_api_risk: Per-site behaviours are exactly what breaks when platforms redesign; social-platform behaviours require continual upkeep.
data_flows: Runs inside the capture browser
opsec_notes: Automated interaction inside a logged-in session looks like bot activity to the platform.
limitations: Only as good as the per-site behaviour coverage.

name: warcio
description: Streaming Python library and CLI for reading, writing, recompressing and checking WARC and legacy ARC files.
journalism_use_case: Programmatically verify, index and extract records from WARC evidence, or convert captures for analysis pipelines.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-10-28 per GitHub API; 486 stars
platform_api_risk: None.
data_flows: Operates on local files only
opsec_notes: Useful for integrity checking before relying on a capture in publication.
limitations: Low-level library; no capture or replay capability of its own.

name: warcprox
description: WARC-writing man-in-the-middle HTTP/S recording proxy: everything routed through it is captured to WARC.
journalism_use_case: Record every request made during a browsing or scraping session into WARC, so collection and evidence capture happen in one pass.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-06-17 per GitHub API; 469 stars; no LICENSE file in repo root (GitHub licence endpoint 404) but pyproject.toml declares license = "GPL-2.0-or-later"
platform_api_risk: Platform-agnostic, but TLS interception breaks on sites using certificate pinning.
external_deps: Python; local CA certificate installed in the browser
data_flows: All proxied traffic, including credentials, is written to your WARCs
opsec_notes: Installing a MITM CA and recording everything means passwords, tokens and unrelated personal browsing can land in WARC files — isolate the profile and treat outputs as sensitive.
limitations: Licence declared only in packaging metadata, not a LICENSE file; operator-level tool.

name: py-wacz
description: Python tool and library for creating and validating WACZ files — zipped, indexed web-archive packages built from WARCs.
journalism_use_case: Package captures into a single self-contained WACZ for archiving, sharing with lawyers, or embedding in a published story.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-10-13 per GitHub API; 63 stars
platform_api_risk: None.
data_flows: Local file packaging only
opsec_notes: Supports signing/validation workflows in the WACZ spec, which helps when provenance is challenged.
limitations: Niche utility, small user base; spec-tracking rather than feature-rich.

name: OutbackCDX
description: Web archive index (CDX) server built on RocksDB, serving capture indexes for Wayback-style replay at scale.
journalism_use_case: Index a large in-house WARC collection so investigators can query by URL and timestamp like the public Wayback Machine.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-13 per GitHub API; 46 stars; canonical repo is iipc/outbackcdx (not nla/outbackcdx)
platform_api_risk: None — serves your own index.
data_flows: Index queries stay within your infrastructure
opsec_notes: Keeps archive lookups internal rather than querying public archives, hiding your research interests.
limitations: Infrastructure component only; requires a pywb/OpenWayback front-end and real ops capacity.

name: Conifer
description: Web archiving platform for collecting and revisiting web pages interactively in a remote browser, the successor to webrecorder.io.
journalism_use_case: Capture a dynamic page or social feed through a remote browser session and keep it in an organised, replayable collection.
deployment: self-hosted docker stack; Rhizome-hosted instance with free tier
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-07-22 per GitHub API; 1,549 stars
platform_api_risk: Remote-browser capture of login-walled platforms requires giving the instance your session, with the usual ToS/account risk.
external_deps: Docker stack; hosted instance storage quotas
data_flows: Captures held by the hosted instance unless you self-host
opsec_notes: Logging into a target platform inside a hosted remote browser exposes that session to the instance operator — self-host for sensitive accounts.
limitations: Slower cadence than Webrecorder's newer tools (4 months since last push); hosted quotas are small.

name: Scoop
description: High-fidelity, browser-based single-page web archiving library and CLI built for 'witnessing' the web, with provenance-oriented capture summaries.
journalism_use_case: Make a defensible, citable capture of one page — the archive-of-record primitive behind Perma.cc-style links.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-09-25 per GitHub API; 217 stars
platform_api_risk: Browser-based, so unaffected by API shutdowns; login-walled content needs credentials and raises ToS issues.
data_flows: WARC/WACZ and attachments written locally
opsec_notes: Designed around provenance (capture summary, timestamps), which strengthens legal defensibility; captures run from your IP.
limitations: Single-page scope by design; not a crawler.

name: Perma
description: The codebase behind Perma.cc, which creates permanent, citable archived copies of web pages for scholarly and legal citation.
journalism_use_case: Preserve cited sources as stable links so a published investigation does not rot when the source page changes or disappears.
deployment: docker-compose self-hosted; primary use is the hosted perma.cc service
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-03 per GitHub API; 540 stars; no LICENSE file in repo root — README 'License' section states dual MIT and GPL-3.0
platform_api_risk: Capture quality on social platforms is limited; hosted service has account tiers and quotas.
external_deps: Django stack, storage; hosted service requires a perma.cc account (institutional tiers)
data_flows: On perma.cc, captures and target URLs are held by Harvard LIL and links are public
opsec_notes: Public Perma links disclose what you archived and when — fine for publication, unsuitable for covert pre-publication research.
limitations: Self-hosting is heavy; licence is declared in README rather than a LICENSE file.

name: SingleFile
description: Browser extension and CLI that saves a faithful copy of a complete web page, including images and styles, as one self-contained HTML file.
journalism_use_case: One-click preservation of a page or social post exactly as rendered in your browser, including content behind a login you legitimately hold.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-13 per GitHub API; 22,925 stars
platform_api_risk: Immune to API shutdowns because it captures the rendered DOM; very widely used for social-post preservation.
data_flows: Saved file written locally; no upload by default
opsec_notes: Captured HTML can embed session-specific content and personal UI artefacts (your name, recommendations) — redact before publishing.
limitations: Not WARC: single HTML snapshots are weaker provenance evidence and lack HTTP headers.

name: monolith
description: CLI and library that bundles a web page and all its assets into a single self-contained HTML file.
journalism_use_case: Scriptable bulk preservation of many URLs as portable single-file snapshots for later reading or diffing.
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-11-13 per GitHub API; 15,608 stars
platform_api_risk: Fetches without a browser engine by default, so JS-rendered social content is often missing.
data_flows: Fetches target assets from your host; writes a local file
opsec_notes: Requests come from your IP with a plain HTTP client; easy to fingerprint as automated.
limitations: No JS execution path for complex pages; not WARC.

name: WebScrapBook
description: Browser extension that captures web pages to local device or a backend server for retrieval, organisation, annotation and editing.
journalism_use_case: Build an annotated personal archive of captured pages, with highlighting and notes kept alongside the evidence.
deployment: browser extension plus optional PyWebScrapBook backend
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-09-28 per GitHub API; 1,251 stars
platform_api_risk: DOM-based capture, so resilient to API changes; dynamic feeds capture only partially.
data_flows: Captures to local disk or your own backend server
opsec_notes: Annotations are stored with captures — avoid writing sensitive investigative hypotheses into files you may later share.
limitations: Single-user tool, idiosyncratic data format, modest ecosystem.

name: shot-scraper
description: CLI for taking automated screenshots of web pages, recording video demos and extracting data from pages via JavaScript.
journalism_use_case: Scheduled visual snapshots of a page (prices, rankings, official notices) to document change over time, plus quick scraping.
deployment: pip CLI; commonly run in GitHub Actions
activity_evidence: Last push 2026-10-14 per GitHub API; 2,608 stars
platform_api_risk: Browser-driven; social platforms may show login walls or anti-bot interstitials in screenshots.
data_flows: Screenshots/JSON written locally or to your CI artefacts
opsec_notes: If run in public GitHub Actions, the target URLs and schedule are publicly visible in your repo.
limitations: Screenshots are weak provenance evidence compared with WARC/WACZ; no replay.
